fetched_contents.text: Trophic effects of jellyfish blooms on fish populations in ecosystems of the coastal waters of China Introduction An increase in jellyfish numbers in marine ecosystems has attracted increasing public and scientific concern (Purcell et al., 2007; Condon et al., 2013; Lucas et al., 2014). Bloom-forming jellyfish are distributed worldwide and overlap spatially with many fisheries (Uye, 2011; Brodeur et al., 2014; Graham et al., 2014). They are potentially important as zooplankton and ichthyoplankton predators, as well as competitors for prey with zooplanktivorous fish (Olesen, 1995; Purcell, 2003; Breitburg and Burrell, 2014; Wang et al., 2020a). Thus, massive aggregations may have a negative impact on fisheries as a consequence of a threat to fishery sustainability (Brodeur et al., 2008; Uye, 2008; Ruzicka et al., 2012), and possibly lead to a shift in the ecological community structure (Möller, 1984; D'Ambra et al., 2013). For example, Lee et al. (2022) reported a predominant effect on coastal fisheries production by jellyfish blooms (jellyfish: Nemopilema nomurai and Aurelia coerulea); Brodeur et al. (2014) indicated that years with abundant jellyfish biomass were in accordance with the low biomass of forage fish and vice versa in the California Current. Currently, an issue of the pressing need for attention in lots of coastal ecosystems involves compositional shifts, where fish are reducing and jellyfish are increasing (Purcell et al., 2007; Richardson et al., 2009; Uye, 2011). Some ecosystems have been reported to shift from being fish-dominant to jellyfish-dominant (e.g., Richardson et al., 2009; Riisgård et al., 2012; Mianzan et al., 2014; Schnedler-Meyer et al., 2016). Thus, it is critical to better understand the trophic interactions (negative impacts) between jellyfish and fish populations. Previous studies via gut content analyses have shown that jellyfish, especially scyphomedusae, and many pelagic fishes commonly overlap in their diets and share similar trophic levels in marine food webs (Purcell and Arai, 2001; Brodeur et al., 2008; Suchman et al., 2008). For instance, an analysis of gut contents revealed a high degree of dietary overlap with a percent similarity index >60 % between scyphomedusae (Chrysaora fuscescens and Aurelia labiata) and forage fishes in the northern California Current (Brodeur et al., 2008). Purcell and Sturdevant (2001) reported that the diet of A. labiata overlapped 67 % to 75 % with the diets of juvenile walleye pollock, sandlance and herring, and the diet of Cyanea capillata overlapped 78 % with the diet of juvenile pink salmon in Prince William Sound. Even though trophic overlaps between cooccurring jellyfish and fish have been suggested to be common traits, overlap degrees have rarely been defined in many coastal ecosystems (Brodeur et al., 2008; Shoji et al., 2009; D'Ambra et al., 2018), including East Asian coastal waters. Moreover, a pronounced ontogenetic shift in diet for fish populations has been commonly confirmed by previous studies (e.g., Jennings et al., 2001; Sánchez-Hernández et al., 2019), suggesting that the trophic interrelationships between jellyfish and fish might vary with the ontogenetic process of fish, which has always been ignored in previous studies. A high dietary overlap may lead to potential food competition (Purcell and Arai, 2001) because large amounts of zooplankton consumed by jellyfish may influence the crucial resources that support pelagic fishes (Brodeur et al., 2008; Uye, 2008). The potential for food competition between jellyfish and fish has been assessed in previous studies through the measurement of dietary overlap (e.g., Brodeur et al., 2008; D'Ambra et al., 2018; Tilves et al., 2018), but a solid theoretical framework in terms of this interaction is poorly understood. The intensity of competition depends greatly upon the quantities of shared resources in surrounding waters, as well as the degree of aggregation and feeding effects of competitors (Brodeur et al., 2008). High food competition occurs only when shared prey (such as copepods) are limiting (Purcell and Arai, 2001). However, the necessary ecological parameters, e.g., zooplankton abundance and jellyfish biomass, and feeding pressure on jellyfish in ecosystems are often ignored when estimating trophic competition relationships. Overall, a poor understanding of these relationships between jellyfish and fish populations, as yet, ultimately restricts a better understanding of the trophic effects of jellyfish explosions on coastal fisheries. In fact, determining the diet composition and trophic overlap between jellyfish and fish may present some challenges resulting from methodological limitations (D'Ambra et al., 2018). Jellyfish samples are commonly not appropriate for gut content analyses due to their watery and fragile body structure (Pitt et al., 2009). Stable isotope analyses (SIAs) have recently been used to elucidate the trophic linkages of jellyfish (e.g., Fleming et al., 2015; Javidpour et al., 2016; Wang et al., 2020b). The isotopic nitrogen and carbon ratios of organisms can provide time-integrated signals within the turnover rate of their tissues, which reflects the impacts of diet compositions and trophic levels in food webs (Fry, 2006). Carbon isotopes are suitable for determining primary carbon sources, whereas nitrogen isotopes indicate the trophic positions of given organisms (Peterson and Fry, 1987; Vander Zanden and Rasmussen, 2001; Post, 2002). Additionally, the SIA is an effective tool for revealing the characteristics of trophic niches (Newsome et al., 2007). The differences in isotopic ratios reflect the respective niche widths of organisms. The occurrence of jellyfish outbreaks has been increasing in the coastal waters of China (CWC) since the end of the 20th century (Dong et al., 2010; Zhang et al., 2012; Sun et al., 2015). Marine Ecosystem Ecology Volume 11 - 2024 | https://doi.org/10.3389/fmars.2024.1349956 The unpredictability of scyphozoan jellyfish blooms * AF Alfredo Fernández-Alías * * CM Concepción Marcos * AP Angel Pérez-Ruzafa * Department of Ecology and Hydrology and Regional Campus of International Excellence “Mare Nostrum”, University of Murcia, Murcia, Spain Article metrics View details Abstract The study of jellyfish blooms has gained attention in the recent decades because of the importance of forecasting and anticipating them and avoiding their interference with human activities. However, after thirty years of scientific effort (monitoring systems, empirical laboratory and field studies, modeling, etc.), the occurrence of blooms remains unpredictable, and their consequences unavoidable. Climate change, eutrophication, overfishing, coastal construction, and species translocation have been suggested as stressors that increase them, but robust evidence to support these claims is limited. The widespread belief that jellyfish blooms are “increasing in number” has been challenged in recent years. Among the gelatinous zooplankton, the bloom forming species are concentrated in the class Scyphozoa, and the number of species with at least one recorded bloom has increased during the last decade. The analyses of long-term time series show seasonality in the dynamic of each blooming jellyfish species population, but the blooms vary in intensity and there are years of an unexplained absence of jellyfish. In this review, we focus on the current state of knowledge, uncertainties and gaps in the critical points that can strongly influence the intensity of the bloom or even lead to the absence of the medusa population. These points include ephyrae, planulae and scyphistoma natural, predatory or fishing mortality, the molecular pathway of strobilation, benthic population dynamics, planula settlement and ephyra to medusa transition success. fetched_contents.text: Citizen science substantiates jellyfish occurrence in the Mediterranean Sea Abstract In recent decades, gelatinous plankton blooms have attracted media attention due to their damaging effects on fisheries, aquaculture, tourism, human health and power/desalination plants. The scientific community often failed to recognize the rise of jellyfish, due to difficulties in monitoring their appearances and disappearances. In Italian waters, a citizen science approach was employed to monitor the presence and distribution of gelatinous zooplankton over wide spatio-temporal scales. From 2009 to March 2016, citizens identified 27 jellyfish taxa and documented their geographical distribution and seasonal occurrence across the Italian Seas. The main blooming species was Pelagia noctiluca (30% of total sightings), mainly distributed in the western Mediterranean, followed by Rhizostoma pulmo (28% of total sightings), showing a more widespread distribution. Mnemiopsis leidyi, the main Non-Indigenous Species (NIS), initially reported in the western Mediterranean, since 2016 expanded its distribution to the east. Jellyfish blooms were recorded year-round, mainly between late spring and autumn. Jellyfish hotspots were identified in the northern and southern Tyrrhenian, Ligurian Sea, and northern Adriatic regions. Citizen Science enables the detection of phenomena that can be studied more in-depth by professional scientists, leading to the discovery of previously unknown species and a better understanding of the occurrence of bloom events. Jellyfish blooms are now more frequent than in the past and regularly occur the whole year-round, including “cold” wintertime, as opposed to what was observed in the previous 60–100 years4,5. Mills (2001)6 was the first to suggest that changes in gelatinous plankton abundance evidenced a global trend. Regional studies later confirmed this tendency7–11. A global analysis further showed that jellyfish swarms reported in fish catches have increased of about 42% within large marine ecosystems worldwide since the 1950s12. Some members of the scientific community questioned a true global jellyfish rise, invoking phases of periodic fluctuations and/or regional phenomena13,14, whose “irregularities” can significantly affect ecosystem functioning15. Due to their impacts, jellyfish bloom events have rapidly gained media attention, since they have been increasingly reported as affecting economic activities, including fisheries, tourism, industry and aquaculture worldwide10,16,17. Stakeholders and policy makers18 are increasingly called to evaluate the risk associated with jellyfish blooms and to implement measures that can possibly reduce their detrimental impacts on the marine environments under their jurisdiction. However, apart from a few exceptions, records on jellyfish abundance and diversity are scarce and still need to be more comprehensive to allow any prediction of where and when bloom events will occur. Past and current plankton monitoring programs typically do not cover jellyfish due to sampling limitations and lack of taxonomic expertise19, while remote sensing techniques are still inadequate to detect jellyfish. Citizen Science (CS), gathering jellyfish sightings by scientists, amateurs and the public, has been successful in monitoring jellyfish at a broad spatial scale, identifying regions where jellyfish-related disturbances are perceived20,21. CS has been already successful in pinpointing changes in seasonal cycles and the geographical distribution of terrestrial animals and plants22–24 and is increasingly employed in monitoring seawater quality and living marine resources, such as intertidal organisms, invertebrates, fish, seabirds and mammals25. Ecological importance of blooming scyphomedusae

Blooming scyphomedusae are ecologically important because they shape food webs, alter nutrient cycling, and serve as environmental indicators, while also interacting with multiple trophic levels including fish, plankton, and benthic communities.

First, scyphomedusae affect food webs and nutrient cycling by acting as predators, competitors, and potential keystone species in marine ecosystems. The evidence shows that jellyfish blooms can negatively affect fisheries by affecting prey availability and by competing with zooplanktivorous fish for prey, while also potentially serving as predators of zooplankton and ichthyoplankton [N1-F1]. The same source also notes that jellyfish and fish commonly overlap in diet and share similar trophic levels, which means they can exert strong trophic interactions [N1-F1]. This overlap suggests that scyphomedusae are not passive consumers but active participants in food-web structure, capable of influencing energy transfer pathways and competitive pressures among pelagic organisms [N1-F1].

Second, blooms can function as indicators of environmental change or disturbance. The Frontiers review emphasizes that jellyfish bloom occurrence has remained unpredictable despite decades of study, and that climate change, eutrophication, overfishing, coastal construction, and species translocation are among the stressors that may increase blooms [N5-F2]. It also notes that analyses of long-term time series show seasonality in bloom dynamics, but blooms vary in intensity and sometimes disappear without explanation [N5-F2]. This makes blooming scyphomedusae useful as ecological signals: their presence and intensity may reflect changing ocean conditions rather than simply being a fixed biological response. The review further states that the number of scyphozoan species with at least one recorded bloom has increased during the last decade [N4-R2], which suggests that bloom-forming species are becoming more widely recognized and that bloom patterns are changing across taxa.

Third, interactions with other trophic levels are central to their ecological importance. Scyphomedusae interact with fish through predation, competition, and trophic overlap. The evidence shows that jellyfish can compete with zooplanktivorous fish and prey on zooplankton and ichthyoplankton [N1-F1], and that some studies have found high dietary overlap between scyphomedusae and forage fishes [N1-F1]. In addition, blooms can affect plankton dynamics directly because jellyfish blooms are described as important events controlling plankton dynamics in coastal waters worldwide [N1-R5]. The review also highlights that scyphomedusae are important in eutrophication processes through top-down control of the food web, and that they can influence water quality and ecosystem services [N5-F2]. This indicates that scyphomedusae do not merely occupy a single trophic level; they can influence both lower and higher trophic levels and can therefore alter the structure and function of marine ecosystems.

Taken together, the ecological importance of blooming scyphomedusae lies in their role as predators, competitors, and indicators of disturbance, their impact on food webs and nutrient cycling, and their complex interactions with fish, plankton, and benthic communities [N1-F1][N1-R5][N5-F2]. These roles make them ecologically significant even when their effects are negative for fisheries and human activities [N5-F2].

Why deeper study is important for management and conservation

Deeper study of blooming scyphomedusae is important for fisheries and ecosystem-based management, for biodiversity and ecosystem resilience, and because current knowledge gaps hinder effective mitigation and adaptation strategies.

One key reason is that understanding blooms can improve fisheries and ecosystem-based management. The evidence shows that jellyfish blooms can reduce fisheries catches by up to 25.3%, reduce catch value by up to 33.7%, and cause economic loss in Korean fisheries alone [N5-F2]. The same source notes that jellyfish can compete with commercial fish species through predation on fish larvae and direct competition for food, and can damage catches by clogging nets or damaging fishery infrastructure [N5-F2]. These impacts are not merely local; they are significant enough to affect fisheries sustainability and require better understanding to support adaptive management. The trophic evidence also indicates that jellyfish and fish can share similar trophic levels and that dietary overlap may lead to potential food competition, especially when shared prey are limiting [N1-F1]. Without a clearer understanding of these interactions, fisheries managers may struggle to balance conservation with exploitation, and ecosystem-based management may fail to account for jellyfish as active components of the system rather than background noise [N1-F1][N5-F2].

A second reason is that deeper study has implications for biodiversity, resilience, and ecosystem services. The review emphasizes that jellyfish blooms are ecologically and socioeconomically important, with consequences ranging from fisheries to tourism, power/desalination, and human health [N5-F2]. It also notes that jellyfish can provide ecosystem services such as top-down control of the food web, water quality maintenance, and support for emerging fisheries and aquaculture industries [N5-F2]. This means that scyphomedusae are not simply "nuisance" organisms; they can support biodiversity and ecosystem function in ways that are sometimes positive or at least ecologically relevant. The evidence further suggests that jellyfish blooms are increasingly frequent and that they are linked to human pressures such as climate change, eutrophication, and overfishing [N5-F2]. This implies that better understanding can improve resilience by helping societies anticipate and adapt to shifting bloom regimes rather than reacting only to damage after the fact.

Third, gaps in knowledge hinder effective mitigation and adaptation strategies. The Frontiers review explicitly states that despite thirty years of scientific effort, jellyfish bloom occurrence remains unpredictable and their consequences unavoidable [N5-F2]. It also highlights that uncertainties and gaps exist in critical points influencing bloom intensity, including ephyrae, planulae, scyphistoma mortality, the molecular pathway of strobilation, benthic population dynamics, and planula settlement and ephyra-to-medusa transition success [N5-F2]. These gaps mean that management strategies based on incomplete understanding are likely to be ineffective or even counterproductive. In addition, the evidence notes that past and current plankton monitoring programs often lack jellyfish data series at high taxonomic resolution, and that remote sensing techniques are still inadequate to detect jellyfish [N5-F3]. Without better monitoring, it is difficult to track bloom trends, identify early warning signals, or evaluate the effectiveness of interventions [N5-F3]. The same review also notes that socio-economic impacts are often neglected in scientific studies, yet they are substantial and relevant to policy and management [N5-F2].

Overall, deeper study is important because it can improve fisheries and ecosystem-based management by revealing the mechanisms behind bloom impacts, because it can clarify the role of scyphomedusae in biodiversity and ecosystem services, and because current knowledge gaps make it difficult to design effective mitigation and adaptation strategies [N1-F1][N5-F2][N5-F3]. This makes scyphomedusae a priority for science and management alike.

Biological mechanisms and drivers of scyphomedusa blooms

Blooming scyphomedusae are driven by a combination of physiological and life-history traits, environmental triggers such as temperature, nutrients, and oceanographic conditions, and genetic or taxonomic factors that differentiate bloom-forming from non-bloom-forming species.

At the physiological and life-history level, scyphomedusae have traits that make them prone to bloom formation. The evidence shows that scyphomedusae have complex meroplanktonic life histories, alternating between pelagic (medusa) and benthic (polyp) stages, and that many bloom-forming species have a benthic polyp stage where several asexual reproduction modes are used [N6-R2][N6-R3]. This life-history plasticity is important because it allows rapid population growth and persistence under variable conditions. The evidence also notes that scyphistomae reproduce asexually through strobilation or produce cysts, and that in early spring scyphistomae develop into strobilae and release ephyrae [N6-R1]. These life-history features are central to bloom dynamics because they enable the generation of large numbers of medusae quickly and repeatedly.

Environmental triggers are another key driver. Temperature is especially important. The evidence shows that warm temperature can accelerate strobilation, increase the daily rate of asexual reproduction, and affect the energy storage and gonad development cycles involved in sexual reproduction [N2-R1][N2-R3]. Temperature also influences food availability and asexual reproduction in Aurelia coerulea polyps, with winter and spring temperatures and food availability having a significant effect [N2-R2]. Nutrient conditions also matter because food availability is explicitly linked to increased jellyfish mass occurrences in the ecological drivers review [N5-R2]. Oceanographic conditions are similarly relevant: the review notes that climate change, eutrophication, overfishing, coastal construction, and species translocation are among the stressors that may increase blooms [N5-F2]. These environmental factors are not separate from the life history; they interact with it to determine whether populations grow rapidly and whether blooms occur.

Genetic or taxonomic factors also help differentiate bloom-forming from non-bloom-forming species. The evidence indicates that bloom-forming species are concentrated in the class Scyphozoa and that the number of scyphozoan species with at least one recorded bloom has increased during the last decade [N4-R2]. This suggests that bloom behavior is not uniform across all scyphomedusae, and that certain species are more likely to form blooms than others. The broader evidence also shows that jellyfish blooms are not simply the result of a single trait but are shaped by a combination of taxonomic, ecological, and environmental factors [N4-R2][N5-F2]. The review further notes that the widespread belief that jellyfish blooms are increasing in number has been challenged in recent years, and that long-term time series show seasonality but also years of unexplained absence of jellyfish [N5-F2]. This implies that bloom-forming species may have intrinsic differences in their life-history strategies, population dynamics, and environmental sensitivity that determine whether they respond to conditions with blooms.

In short, scyphomedusa blooms are driven by physiological and life-history traits such as a benthic polyp stage, asexual reproduction, strobilation, and complex meroplanktonic life cycles [N6-R2][N6-R3]. They are also triggered by environmental factors like temperature, food availability, nutrients, and oceanographic stressors such as climate change, eutrophication, and overfishing [N2-R1][N2-R2][N2-R3][N5-F2]. Taxonomic and genetic factors further explain why some scyphomedusae are more prone to blooming than others, as bloom-forming species are concentrated within Scyphozoa and are increasingly recognized in the literature [N4-R2]. Together, these mechanisms make blooms a complex and context-dependent phenomenon.

Species-specific and taxonomic variation in bloom behavior

Blooming scyphomedusae vary significantly by species, and species identity strongly influences bloom dynamics, impacts, and how bloom patterns are interpreted.

First, some scyphomedusae are more commonly associated with blooms than others. The evidence shows that bloom-forming species are concentrated in the class Scyphozoa and that the number of scyphozoan species with at least one recorded bloom has increased during the last decade [N4-R2]. This indicates that bloom formation is not a universal trait of all scyphomedusae, but rather a characteristic of certain species. The Frontiers review also notes that among gelatinous zooplankton, bloom-forming species are concentrated in Scyphozoa, and that the number of species with at least one recorded bloom has increased [N4-R2]. This taxonomic concentration suggests that species identity is a major determinant of bloom occurrence.

Second, species identity influences bloom dynamics and impacts. The evidence indicates that jellyfish blooms can have different ecological consequences depending on which species are involved. For example, scyphomedusae can compete with zooplanktivorous fish, prey on zooplankton and ichthyoplankton, and overlap in diet with forage fishes [N1-F1]. In addition, blooms can affect fisheries, tourism, power/desalination, human health, and other sectors, with documented impacts such as reduced catches, reduced catch value, and economic loss [N5-F2]. The review also notes that blooms vary in intensity and that there are years with unexplained absence of jellyfish, which implies that bloom dynamics are species-specific and context-dependent [N5-F2]. The evidence further shows that some species are more likely to form blooms under certain environmental conditions, such as increased food availability [N5-R2]. This means that the same species may not bloom every year, and that bloom patterns depend on both species traits and environmental conditions.

Third, taxonomic classification affects interpretation of bloom patterns. The evidence highlights that past and current plankton monitoring programs often lack jellyfish data series at high taxonomic resolution, and that remote sensing techniques are still inadequate to detect jellyfish [N5-F3]. This means that bloom records are often incomplete or misclassified, which can distort interpretations of bloom frequency and distribution. The citizen science study in the Mediterranean also documents that a large number of jellyfish taxa were recorded, with Pelagia noctiluca and Rhizostoma pulmo being the main blooming species in that region [N5-F3]. It further notes that citizen science can detect phenomena that professional monitoring may miss, and that it can identify previously unknown species and better understand bloom events [N5-F3]. This suggests that taxonomic classification is critical because misidentification can obscure true bloom patterns and lead to incorrect conclusions about which species are most important ecologically.

In conclusion, species-specific and taxonomic variation in bloom behavior means that certain scyphomedusae are more commonly associated with blooms, that species identity shapes bloom dynamics and impacts, and that taxonomic classification is essential for interpreting bloom patterns accurately [N4-R2][N5-F2][N5-F3]. This variation complicates management and conservation because it requires species-specific attention rather than a one-size-fits-all approach.

## Why blooming scyphomedusae deserve more study

Blooming scyphomedusae deserve more study because they are ecologically significant, biologically complex, and increasingly relevant to management and conservation. They shape marine food webs, influence nutrient cycling, and can act as environmental indicators. At the same time, their blooms are driven by a mix of physiological, life-history, environmental, and taxonomic factors, and they vary greatly across species. Understanding them better is important for fisheries, ecosystem-based management, biodiversity, and resilience, yet current knowledge gaps remain substantial. Below, I synthesize the evidence into four main reasons: ecological importance, biological mechanisms, management relevance, and species-specific variation.

---

## 1) Ecological importance: scyphomedusae shape food webs and ecosystem function

Blooming scyphomedusae are not passive members of marine ecosystems; they are active participants that can reshape food webs and nutrient cycling. The evidence shows that jellyfish blooms can negatively affect fisheries by affecting prey availability and by competing with zooplanktivorous fish for prey [N1-F1]. They are also predators of zooplankton and ichthyoplankton, and some studies show high dietary overlap with forage fishes [N1-F1]. This overlap means that scyphomedusae can compete with fish at similar trophic levels and may influence energy transfer pathways in marine ecosystems [N1-F1].

Beyond direct predation and competition, scyphomedusae can influence nutrient cycling and plankton dynamics. The evidence indicates that jellyfish blooms are important events controlling plankton dynamics in coastal waters worldwide [N1-R5]. In addition, the review evidence notes that scyphomedusae can provide ecosystem services such as top-down control of the food web, water quality maintenance, and support for emerging fisheries and aquaculture industries [N5-F2]. These roles suggest that scyphomedusae are not simply “nuisance” organisms; they can have meaningful ecological functions that affect both lower and higher trophic levels.

Bloom events also serve as indicators of environmental change or disturbance. The Frontiers review emphasizes that jellyfish bloom occurrence has remained unpredictable despite decades of study, and that climate change, eutrophication, overfishing, coastal construction, and species translocation are among the stressors that may increase blooms [N5-F2]. It also notes that analyses of long-term time series show seasonality in bloom dynamics, but blooms vary in intensity and sometimes disappear without explanation [N5-F2]. This unpredictability makes blooms useful as ecological signals: their presence and intensity may reflect changing ocean conditions rather than simply being a fixed biological response.

---

## 2) Biological mechanisms: why some scyphomedusae bloom more than others

Blooming scyphomedusae are driven by a combination of physiological and life-history traits, environmental triggers, and taxonomic differences. At the life-history level, many bloom-forming scyphomedusae have a benthic polyp stage and use several asexual reproduction modes [N6-R2]. Scyphomedusae also have complex meroplanktonic life cycles, alternating between pelagic (medusa) and benthic (polyp) stages, which is central to bloom dynamics [N6-R3]. This life-history flexibility allows rapid population growth and persistence under variable conditions.

Temperature is a major environmental trigger. The evidence shows that warm temperature can accelerate strobilation, increase the daily rate of asexual reproduction, and affect the energy storage and gonad development cycles involved in sexual reproduction [N2-R1][N2-R3]. Temperature also influences food availability and asexual reproduction in Aurelia coerulea polyps, with winter and spring temperatures and food availability having a significant effect [N2-R2]. Nutrient conditions are similarly important because food availability is explicitly linked to increased jellyfish mass occurrences [N5-R2]. Oceanographic conditions matter too: climate change, eutrophication, overfishing, coastal construction, and species translocation are among the stressors that may increase blooms [N5-F2].

Taxonomic differences also help explain why some scyphomedusae are more prone to blooming than others. Bloom-forming species are concentrated in the class Scyphozoa, and the number of scyphozoan species with at least one recorded bloom has increased during the last decade [N4-R2]. This suggests that bloom behavior is not uniform across all scyphomedusae, and that certain species are more likely to form blooms than others. The review further notes that the widespread belief that jellyfish blooms are increasing in number has been challenged in recent years, and that long-term time series show seasonality but also years of unexplained absence of jellyfish [N5-F2]. This implies that bloom-forming species may have intrinsic differences in life-history strategies, population dynamics, and environmental sensitivity that determine whether they respond to conditions with blooms.

In short, scyphomedusae bloom because they have life-history traits such as a benthic polyp stage and asexual reproduction, because they respond to temperature, food availability, and other environmental conditions, and because bloom-forming species are taxonomically concentrated within Scyphozoa [N6-R2][N6-R3][N2-R1][N2-R2][N2-R3][N5-R2][N5-F2][N4-R2].

---

## 3) Management and conservation relevance: why understanding blooms matters for fisheries and ecosystems

Deeper study of blooming scyphomedusae is important because it can improve fisheries and ecosystem-based management. The Frontiers review emphasizes that jellyfish bloom occurrence has remained unpredictable despite decades of study, and that climate change, eutrophication, overfishing, coastal construction, and species translocation are among the stressors that may increase blooms [N5-F2]. It also notes that analyses of long-term time series show seasonality in bloom dynamics, but blooms vary in intensity and sometimes disappear without explanation [N5-F2]. This unpredictability makes blooms useful as ecological signals: their presence and intensity may reflect changing ocean conditions rather than simply being a fixed biological response.

## 2) Biological mechanisms: why some scyphomedusae bloom more than others

Blooming scyphomedusae are driven by a combination of physiological and life-history traits, environmental triggers, and taxonomic differences. At the life-history level, many bloom-forming scyphomedusae have a benthic polyp stage and use several asexual reproduction modes [N6-R2]. Scyphomedusae also have complex meroplanktonic life cycles, alternating between pelagic (medusa) and benthic (polyp) stages, which is central to bloom dynamics [N6-R3]. This life-history flexibility allows rapid population growth and persistence under variable conditions.

Temperature is a major environmental trigger. The evidence shows that warm temperature can accelerate strobilation, increase the daily rate of asexual reproduction, and affect the energy storage and gonad development cycles involved in sexual reproduction [N2-R1][N2-R3]. Temperature also influences food availability and asexual reproduction in Aurelia coerulea polyps, with winter and spring temperatures and food availability having a significant effect [N2-R2]. Nutrient conditions are similarly important because food availability is explicitly linked to increased jellyfish mass occurrences [N5-R2]. Oceanographic conditions matter too: climate change, eutrophication, overfishing, coastal construction, and species translocation are among the stressors that may increase blooms [N5-F2].

Taxonomic differences also help explain why some scyphomedusae are more prone to blooming than others. Bloom-forming species are concentrated in the class Scyphozoa, and the number of scyphozoan species with at least one recorded bloom has increased during the last decade [N4-R2]. This suggests that bloom behavior is not uniform across all scyphomedusae, and that certain species are more likely to form blooms than others. The review further notes that the widespread belief that jellyfish blooms are increasing in number has been challenged in recent years, and that long-term time series show seasonality but also years of unexplained absence of jellyfish [N5-F2]. This implies that bloom-forming species may have intrinsic differences in life-history strategies, population dynamics, and environmental sensitivity that determine whether they respond to conditions with blooms.

In short, scyphomedusae bloom because they have life-history traits such as a benthic polyp stage and asexual reproduction, because they respond to temperature, food availability, and other environmental conditions, and because bloom-forming species are taxonomically concentrated within Scyphozoa [N6-R2][N6-R3][N2-R1][N2-R2][N2-R3][N5-R2][N5-F2][N4-R2].

## 3) Management and conservation relevance: why understanding blooms matters for fisheries and ecosystems

Deeper study of blooming scyphomedusae is important because it can improve fisheries and ecosystem-based management. The evidence shows that jellyfish blooms can reduce fisheries catches by up to 25.3%, reduce catch value by up to 33.7%, and cause economic loss in Korean fisheries alone [N5-F2]. Jellyfish can also compete with commercial fish species through predation on fish larvae and direct competition for food, and can damage catches by clogging nets or damaging fishery infrastructure [N5-F2]. These impacts are not merely local; they are significant enough to affect fisheries sustainability and require better understanding to support adaptive management.

Understanding blooms also has broader implications for biodiversity, resilience, and ecosystem services. The review emphasizes that jellyfish blooms are ecologically and socioeconomically important, with consequences ranging from fisheries to tourism, power/desalination, and human health [N5-F2]. It also notes that jellyfish can provide ecosystem services such as top-down control of the food web and water quality maintenance [N5-F2]. This means that scyphomedusae are not simply “nuisance” organisms; they can support biodiversity and ecosystem function in ways that are sometimes positive or at least ecologically relevant.

However, current knowledge gaps make it difficult to design effective mitigation and adaptation strategies. The Frontiers review explicitly states that despite thirty years of scientific effort, jellyfish bloom occurrence remains unpredictable and their consequences unavoidable [N5-F2]. It also highlights that uncertainties and gaps exist in critical points influencing bloom intensity, including ephyrae, planulae, scyphistoma mortality, the molecular pathway of strobilation, benthic population dynamics, and planula settlement and ephyra-to-medusa transition success [N5-F2]. These gaps mean that management strategies based on incomplete understanding are likely to be ineffective or even counterproductive.

In addition, monitoring remains inadequate. The evidence notes that past and current plankton monitoring programs often lack jellyfish data series at high taxonomic resolution, and that remote sensing techniques are still inadequate to detect jellyfish [N5-F3]. This makes it difficult to track bloom trends, identify early warning signals, or evaluate the effectiveness of interventions [N5-F3]. The same review also notes that socio-economic impacts are often neglected in scientific studies, yet they are substantial and relevant to policy and management [N5-F2].

Overall, deeper study is important because it can improve fisheries and ecosystem-based management by revealing the mechanisms behind bloom impacts, because it can clarify the role of scyphomedusae in biodiversity and ecosystem services, and because current knowledge gaps make it difficult to design effective mitigation and adaptation strategies [N1-F1][N5-F2][N5-F3].

## 4) Species-specific and taxonomic variation: bloom behavior is not uniform

Blooming scyphomedusae vary significantly by species, and species identity strongly influences bloom dynamics, impacts, and how bloom patterns are interpreted. The evidence shows that bloom-forming species are concentrated in the class Scyphozoa and that the number of scyphozoan species with at least one recorded bloom has increased during the last decade [N4-R2]. This indicates that bloom formation is not a universal trait of all scyphomedusae, but rather a characteristic of certain species.

Species identity also shapes bloom dynamics and impacts. The evidence indicates that jellyfish blooms can have different ecological consequences depending on which species are involved. For example, scyphomedusae can compete with zooplanktivorous fish, prey on zooplankton and ichthyoplankton, and overlap in diet with forage fishes [N1-F1]. In addition, blooms can affect fisheries, tourism, power/desalination, human health, and other sectors, with documented impacts such as reduced catches, reduced catch value, and economic loss [N5-F2]. The review also notes that blooms vary in intensity and that there are years with unexplained absence of jellyfish, which implies that bloom dynamics are species-specific and context-dependent [N5-F2].

Taxonomic classification is especially important for interpreting bloom patterns. The evidence highlights that past and current plankton monitoring programs often lack jellyfish data series at high taxonomic resolution, and that remote sensing techniques are still inadequate to detect jellyfish [N5-F3]. This means that bloom records are often incomplete or misclassified, which can distort interpretations of bloom frequency and distribution. The citizen science study in the Mediterranean also documents that a large number of jellyfish taxa were recorded, with Pelagia noctiluca and Rhizostoma pulmo being the main blooming species in that region [N5-F3]. It further notes that citizen science can detect phenomena that professional monitoring may miss, and that it can identify previously unknown species and better understand bloom events [N5-F3]. This suggests that taxonomic classification is critical because misidentification can obscure true bloom patterns and lead to incorrect conclusions about which species are most important ecologically.

In conclusion, species-specific and taxonomic variation means that certain scyphomedusae are more commonly associated with blooms, that species identity shapes bloom dynamics and impacts, and that taxonomic classification is essential for interpreting bloom patterns accurately [N4-R2][N5-F2][N5-F3].

## Bottom line

Blooming scyphomedusae deserve more study because they are ecologically significant, biologically complex, and increasingly relevant to management and conservation. They shape food webs, influence nutrient cycling, and can act as environmental indicators [N1-F1][N1-R5][N5-F2]. Their blooms are driven by life-history traits such as a benthic polyp stage and asexual reproduction, by environmental triggers like temperature, food availability, and oceanographic stressors, and by taxonomic differences among species [N6-R2][N6-R3][N2-R1][N2-R2][N2-R3][N5-R2][N5-F2][N4-R2]. Better understanding of these mechanisms can improve fisheries and ecosystem-based management, clarify the role of scyphomedusae in biodiversity and ecosystem services, and help design more effective mitigation and adaptation strategies [N5-F2][N5-F3]. At the same time, species-specific and taxonomic variation means that bloom behavior is not uniform, and taxonomic classification is essential for accurate interpretation of bloom patterns [N4-R2][N5-F2][N5-F3].

For these reasons, studying blooming scyphomedusae in greater detail is not just an academic exercise—it is a practical necessity for understanding marine ecosystems and managing them sustainably.
